we are creating "yolo-twice" a tool to help individuals and teams get insights into long running claude code sessions.

The basic idea is to inspect and visualize long running conversations on the fly as they evolve and present different levels of abstraction of the transcript that allow the user to easily navigate and search the history and deep dive where they choose to. This could include interactive, time line, text search, flow graph, strechtext like semantic abstraction levels, semantic clusters etc

we can imagine a solution that has an seperate engine running that watches and indexes the users relevant  ~/.claude/* folders, transforms fil system changes into and event stream and analysis and transforms the events using local tools and eventually claude code itself. the UI could be a web UI, updated in real time. Indexing must work incrementally, so it can we stopped, resumed.

In order to keep and share the history yolo-twice shall store all state into the projects .yolo-twice folder so it can be commited with the project or gitignored.

Design principles: idempotency

claude code user could have commands in the cli like
- /yolo-twice (opens the insights UI for the current project folder, launches engine if needed )
- /yolo-twice stop ( stops the engine) 

There must be a github pages website and a readme explaining the installation as single commmand.
Our idea is to ship yolo-twice as claude plugin / mcp so first interaction is through claude cli.

We will also generate a 3 min pitch presentation, which might reuse elements of the githib page. both sould be very simple and use graphical elements as mermaid diagrams.

use open standards and protocols wherever possible. We wrote everything for claude code in this prompt but also want to extend to other coding agents like opencode in the future.

We are 4 people and want to work AI driven in parallel so a modular design would help us.

Challange our ideas. consider options and improve the idea. Search for inspiration in similar projects. Maybe we can reuse or extend working approaches.

I found several open-source Claude Code transcript viewers on GitHub, each with a different focus:

- **cc_transcript_viewer (tim-hua-01):** A zero-dependency local web app. It also covers Codex, Cursor, and opencode, and it refreshes live so you can follow an active session. It can also export a session as a standalone HTML file. (git clone https://github.com/tim-hua-01/cc_transcript_viewer.git)
- **Claudescope (vladar107):** A local viewer and search tool that also handles six other agents. It offers full-text search, tool-call views, token and cost analytics, and Markdown export. It is MIT licensed. (It reads Claude Code session transcripts and makes them browsable, searchable, and comparable against other agents' sessions.) The repo is at https://github.com/vladar107/claudescope.
- **claude-code-viewer (esc5221):** A desktop app that renders transcripts with Markdown and syntax highlighting. It is MIT licensed and built with Node.js. (npm run dist:mac is one of its build commands.)
- **claude-code-transcripts (simonw, also a fork by ricklupton):** A Python CLI that turns sessions into paginated HTML pages, with an option to publish to a GitHub Gist. (It converts Claude Code session files (JSON or JSONL) into mobile-friendly HTML pages with pagination.)
- **claude-transcript-viewer (varunr89):** A web server with search and infinite scroll. It is MIT licensed and can be run with npx. (It is a web server for browsing and searching Claude Code conversation transcripts with semantic search, infinite scroll, and collapsible cells.)
- **claude-scrollback (alexdej):** A lightweight viewer with a session browser and static HTML generation. It also adds a resume command for each session.
- **claude-reader (vikasgrac):** A terminal pane that tails the live transcript and shows only the prose you need to read, without the tool-call noise.
- **Claude Code Helper (yaiol):** A two-pane viewer that merges sessions from Windows and WSL distributions. Its licensing is not stated in the results.

**OpenCode session storage**

- **Current format:** Sources disagree on the exact layout. A SKILL.md guide and a txcript format doc both describe a single SQLite database at `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`, with session, message, and part tables. txcript also notes that `$XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/opencode.db` takes precedence when that variable is set, and that an `OPENCODE_DB` env var can override it.
- **Legacy format:** txcript's doc mentions a legacy JSON `storage/` tree that was migrated. A Raycast extension still reads from `~/.local/share/opencode/storage` by default, and a codetether module parses per-session JSON files under `storage/session/`. So older installs may still have JSON files.
- **Exports:** The built-in `/export` reportedly writes only the messages loaded in the TUI, so long sessions can be truncated. One community plugin reads the SQLite store directly and writes Markdown, and another writes transcripts to a `convos/` folder on session idle.

**Agent Trace open standard**

- The Agent Trace spec (agent-trace.dev) is a vendor-neutral format for recording which code in a version-controlled repo came from AI versus humans, including the related agent conversations. It is a data spec, version 0.1.0, status RFC, dated January 2026. Cursor's proposal is the origin, per a post by one of its supporters.
- Other "trace" standards are unrelated and could be confused with it. These include TRACE (trace-spec, a signed attestation receipt for agent runs, v0.2 developer preview, under the Linux Foundation), OpenTrace (a runtime tracing spec for agent systems), and OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions.

I did not verify whether OpenCode writes Agent Trace records. I'd need a search on OpenCode and agent-trace together to check that.

The search turned up no coding-agent-specific conventions. The general GenAI agent conventions are the closest match, and the sources disagree on maturity.

- **Status is contested.** Most sources say the conventions are still in Development. One says the repository currently marks the GenAI conventions as Development, and as of August 21, 2026 it has no official release. Another reports the OTel GenAI SIG has stabilized the GenAI Semantic Conventions in June 2026, but it is a secondary blog and the other sources don't corroborate it. Treat the Development status as the better-supported reading.
- **Repository move.** Core v1.42.0 moved the GenAI definitions into the separate semantic-conventions-genai repository.
- **Agent operations.** The agent conventions define operations such as create_agent, invoke_agent, invoke_workflow, plan, and execute_tool. One source says v1.41 split invoke_agent into CLIENT/INTERNAL span kinds.
- **Tool calls and MCP.** MCP has its own Development conventions for client and server spans, W3C Trace Context propagation, transport correlation, tool-aware attributes, and metrics. The agent metrics include gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.tool.name, and gen_ai.tool.status, though that source is the less reliable one.
- **Content and evaluation.** Prompt and output capture is Opt-In, and the OpenTelemetry documentation warns that event support is not yet available in every language. For evaluator results, gen_ai.evaluation.result provides a standard carrier for evaluator scores and explanations.

Nothing I found addresses coding agents such as Claude Code specifically. The sources cover general agent and LLM tracing.

**Claudescope** (vladar107/claudescope) is a local, read-only viewer for AI coding-agent transcripts.

- **Supported agents (8):** Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, JetBrains Junie, pi, opencode, GitHub Copilot CLI, Google Antigravity, and xAI Grok CLI. Each source is optional, and sessions are grouped by project with an agent tag.

- **Indexing:** The app re-scans on an interval (default 15 seconds) and incrementally picks up new or changed transcripts without a restart. Unchanged scans are cheap, and `POST /api/reindex` forces one. The page doesn't describe filesystem watching. Ranked full-text search can lag a live session by up to a minute.

- **Storage:** Its own index is a DuckDB database, not SQLite. It reads opencode's SQLite database read-only through Node's built-in `node:sqlite`. Other state includes a pricing file and a settings file, all under `~/.claudescope/`.

- **Features:**
  - Browsing projects and sessions, with token, cost, and PR details
  - A threaded session reader with diffs, subagent runs, and in-session find
  - A "Files changed" tab
  - Markdown export with optional redaction
  - A memory viewer for instruction files and per-project memory
  - An inventory of skills, MCP servers, hooks, and plugins
  - Full-text search across all agents, with an exact-match mode
  - Token and cost analytics by time, project, model, and agent
  - A cross-agent efficiency comparison and a weekly digest
  - An MCP server, a CLI with JSON output, a Claude Code/Codex plugin, and a Raycast extension

  The page doesn't describe a dedicated timeline view. Analytics "over time" and the digest are the closest equivalents.

- **Tech stack:** Node.js 22.13+, TypeScript, DuckDB (`@duckdb/node-api`), Vitest, and npm. It's distributed through npm, Homebrew, and Nix, and it runs a local server on `127.0.0.1`.

- A single time-sorted sidebar across all sources, with agent, model, directory, and date filters and content search.
- Transcript rendering with Markdown, LaTeX, images, collapsible thinking blocks, and tool-specific formatting, including diffs.
- Sub-agent and guardian linking, a prompt outline, and jump controls.

- Exporters that convert Cursor and opencode sessions into Codex rollout format.

**Live refresh**

The sidebar rescans about once per second. An open transcript is checked about three times per second and tails in place while keeping scroll position and expanded blocks. Session metadata is cached by file modification time, so each poll only re-reads changed files. For opencode, change detection also watches the write-ahead log.

Python 3.9+ with only the standard library on the server, and vanilla JavaScript with no build step on the frontend. I have enough context now. Here is what I found, where I'd push back, and the questions I need answered before writing a plan.

**What I found**

- **This is BaselHack 2026**, which runs 30 Oct to 1 Nov, so you have roughly a day. The readme is the BaselHack template. That deadline should drive every scope decision below.
- **The viewer space is crowded.** I found over a dozen Claude Code transcript viewers. Three are serious: [Claudescope](https://github.com/vladar107/claudescope) covers 8 agents with DuckDB search, cost analytics and an MCP server plus Claude plugin. [claude-code-history-viewer](https://github.com/jhlee0409/claude-code-history-viewer) covers 31 agents with file watching and SSE live updates. [cc_transcript_viewer](https://github.com/tim-hua-01/cc_transcript_viewer) is zero-dependency with live tail. All are MIT.
- **None of them do** semantic abstraction levels, semantic clustering, a flow graph of the conversation tree, or project-local shareable state. That gap is your pitch. Timeline, search and cost analytics alone will not win.
- **The transcript is a tree, not a list.** Each record links to its parent, rewinds create branches, subagents live in their own JSONL files next to the session, and compaction leaves summary markers. Branches, subagent nesting and compaction boundaries are free abstraction levels you can show without any LLM call.
- **Hooks beat filesystem watching as the event source.** Claude Code exposes 33 hook events, each delivering the session id, transcript path, cwd and agent id. A plugin can ship them. The docs warn the transcript file lags the live conversation, so hooks should trigger reads of the JSONL, not replace it.
- **Open standards exist but none fit cleanly.** Claude Code exports OpenTelemetry logs natively, but prompt content is opt-in and config is read at startup. The OTel GenAI conventions are still in Development status. ACP from Zed can replay a session via session/load, and opencode speaks ACP, but Claude Code needs an adapter. opencode stores sessions in a single SQLite database, a different model entirely.
- **Single-command install is realistic.** Your local CLI supports the plugin install command directly, so the README line can be a marketplace add plus install.

**Where I challenge the idea**

- **Watching all of ~/.claude is wrong for a project tool.** Scope the engine to the current project's session folder. The rest is other projects' private data.
- **Committing `.yolo-twice` to git is a privacy trap.** Transcripts contain pasted secrets and tool output. Store only derived artifacts there, in plain JSON files rather than a binary database so git diffs and merges work, with an explicit export step for sharing.
- **Define idempotency concretely.** Key every derived artifact by the hash of its input records plus the analyzer version. Re-running produces byte-identical files, which is what makes stop and resume trivial.
- **LLM analysis during indexing is the biggest risk** for a day-long hackathon. Branch and compaction structure, tool-call grouping and BM25 search give you three abstraction levels with zero LLM cost. Add LLM summaries only on top, via the headless `claude -p` command so no API key is needed.
- **Build the parser on an existing MIT project** rather than from scratch. Claudescope's Node parser or cc_transcript_viewer's Python one already handle subagents, sidechains and tool results.

**Questions I cannot answer myself**

1. Who is the primary user in the demo: a developer reviewing their own long session, or a team lead reviewing a colleague's?
2. Should `.yolo-twice` ever contain raw transcript copies, or only derived summaries, indexes and annotations?
3. Are LLM calls during indexing acceptable, and if so via subscription through the headless CLI or via an API key?
4. Pitch format: a Markdown deck rendered on the same GitHub Pages site, or a PowerPoint from the corporate template?
5. What does the name "yolo-twice" mean, and are there branding constraints?
6. Do you want me to propose the four-person module split, or do you already have one?

Edit freely. ## 1. Context Long Claude Code sessions are black boxes: a single session JSONL grows to megabytes, spawns subagent transcripts, branches on rewind and gets compacted. Existing viewers render this as a flat chat list. yolo-twice makes a running session navigable at several levels of abstraction, live, and stores what it learns next to the project so it can be committed or ignored. Built at BaselHack 2026 (30 Oct to 1 Nov) by four people working AI-driven in parallel. Demo on 1 Nov is a vertical slice; the architecture is designed for the full vision. ### Decisions taken | Topic | Decision | |---|---| | Deadline | Demo slice on 1 Nov, continue afterwards | | Pitch features | Semantic zoom, live flow graph, shareable project history. Cross-agent later | | Event source | Claude Code hooks trigger ingestion; the session JSONL is the source of truth; file watcher as fallback | | Stack | Node/TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces) | | Primary user | Developer reviewing their own sessions; team sharing is a later layer on the same data | | `.yolo-twice` content | Redacted raw events plus derived data, so it is safe to commit | | LLM analysis | Headless `claude -p` through the user's subscription, hash-cached, never blocking the UI | | Pitch | Markdown deck on GitHub Pages, reusing the site's mermaid diagrams | ### What exists and what we add Over a dozen Claude Code transcript viewers exist. The strongest are [Claudescope](https://github.com/vladar107/claudescope) (8 agents, DuckDB search, MCP server, plugin), [claude-code-history-viewer](https://github.com/jhlee0409/claude-code-history-viewer) (31 agents, file watch, SSE) and [cc_transcript_viewer](https://github.com/tim-hua-01/cc_transcript_viewer) (zero dependencies, live tail). zoom, flow graph, timeline, search] PLUGIN[Claude plugin
/yolo-twice, /yolo-twice stop] --> ENG ``` ### Packages (monorepo under `code/`) | Package | Responsibility | Owner | |---|---|---| | `packages/core` | Event schema, source adapters (claude-code now, opencode later), redaction, cursor-based incremental reader, `.yolo-twice` store | A | | `packages/engine` | Daemon: HTTP API, SSE stream, `/hook` endpoint, watcher fallback, analyzer queue, pid/port lifecycle, CLI (`yolo-twice start|stop|status|index`) | A | | `packages/analyzers` | Structural tree (L0 to L4), full-text search, semantic phase summaries and cluster labels via `claude -p`, cost rollups | B | | `packages/ui` | Vite + React web app: zoom view (stretchtext), flow graph, timeline, search, live updates over SSE | C | | `plugin/` | Claude Code plugin: `plugin.json`, `commands/yolo-twice.md`, `hooks/hooks.json`, `bin/yolo-twice` | D | | `site/` and `assets/pitch/` | VitePress site and Slidev deck, both with native mermaid, deployed to GitHub Pages by one Actions workflow | D | | `fixtures/` | Two or three real sessions, redacted, so B and C can develop without the engine running | D | ## 3. Live pipeline ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant CC as Claude Code participant H as hook (HTTP) participant E as Engine participant S as .yolo-twice participant UI as Web UI CC->>H: UserPromptSubmit / PostToolUse / SubagentStop / PostCompact / Stop H->>E: POST /hook {session_id, transcript_path, agent_id, hook_event_name} E->>E: debounce 300 ms per transcript E->>S: read new lines from cursor, normalize, redact, append events.ndjson E->>S: update structure.json (structural levels, no LLM) E-->>UI: SSE: events, structure E->>E: enqueue semantic jobs for changed phases (hash-keyed) E->>S: write semantic/.json when claude -p returns E-->>UI: SSE: semantic ``` The transcript file lags the live conversation, so every hook triggers a re-read from the cursor and the next hook or watcher event picks up anything missed. Good question, and it exposes something the design glossed over: not all layers cost the same, so the slider should not throttle everything uniformly.

**Where the cost actually sits**

| Layer | Cost per event | Realtime safe? |
|---|---|---|
| Ingest, normalize, redact, append | microseconds, linear in new bytes | yes, always |
| Structural tree and search index | milliseconds, incremental | yes |
| Flow graph re-layout in the browser | noticeable with thousands of nodes | throttle |
| Semantic summaries via `claude -p` | seconds to minutes, thousands of tokens, one Node process spawn | no |
| Pushing updates at the user | attention, not CPU | this is the real "micro management" |

The expensive layer is semantic work, and it has a trap: re-summarizing an open phase after every turn is quadratic in tokens over the phase, and every interim result is a cache miss by design because the input hash keeps changing. It also competes with your own Claude Code session for the same subscription rate limit, which is a strong argument against eager summarization as the default.

**So yes, give the choice, but make the slider control triggers and attention, not ingestion**

Ingestion always runs near realtime because it is nearly free. That way the data is always complete and zooming in is instant regardless of mode. The slider decides when semantic work is triggered and how much the UI pushes at you. I'd use a slider with four detents rather than a continuous value, since the modes are qualitatively different and need testing:

| Detent | Semantic trigger | Default zoom | UI behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Micro management | every turn, incremental fold summary of the open phase with a small model | L3 steps | live ticker, graph re-layout batched to 1 s |
| Attentive | turn label on each Stop hook, phase summary when a phase closes | L2 turns | live, no interim phase summaries |
| Balanced (default) | phase close only: compaction, idle gap, topic change | L1 phases | updates on phase boundaries |
| Yolo | nothing automatic; summaries computed lazily when the UI shows the node, or on SessionEnd | L0 digest | "catch me up" button summarizes everything since you last looked |

Two details make this clean:

- **Viewport is the demand signal.** The UI requests summaries for visible nodes. Yolo is pure lazy, micro is eager prefetch of everything. Same code path, different prefetch policy.
- **Idempotency survives the slider.** A closed phase has the same input hash in every mode, so the artifact is identical whether it was computed eagerly or lazily. Interim summaries of open phases are marked `interim` and written to the gitignored cache, never to the committed sessions folder. Switching modes never produces conflicting committed files.

The "catch me up" digest is the strongest feature of yolo mode and fits the pitch: you let the agent run, go for coffee, and come back to a summary of what happened since your last look, from the engine's last-viewed cursor.

Show the cost next to the slider: an estimated tokens-per-hour and update lag readout, so the tradeoff is explicit rather than hidden. The setting lives in the project config with a per-user override, is changeable live from the UI header or `/yolo-twice mode yolo`, and the engine reloads it without restart.

| Level | Unit | Source | LLM needed |
|---|---|---|---|

| L4 | Raw record | JSONL line | no |

**Text axis** (how much text a node shows), in the stretchtext sense: any text can be
collapsed in place to a shorter form and expanded back.

| Granularity | Target | Example at L0 |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | one line | "Migrated auth to OIDC, tests green" |
| `abstract` | up to three sentences | what, why, outcome |

one step further shows the project as a list of session titles, which can itself be
summarized into a project digest. Zooming in on a long tool result or a long assistant

## Inline shell execution (`` !`command` ``)

Claude Code runs the command before the content is sent to Claude, and the output replaces the placeholder:

```markdown
## Current changes

!`git diff HEAD`
```

- The inline form is recognized only when `!` is at the start of a line or follows whitespace. In `KEY=!`cmd``, it stays literal and doesn't run.
- For multi-line commands, use a fenced block opened with ` ```! `:

  ````markdown
  ```!
  node --version
  git status --short
  ```
  ````
- A non-zero exit code aborts the whole invocation, and Claude never sees the content. Exit code 1 from search and comparison commands is the exception. To tolerate other failures, append `|| true`.
- Output is inserted as plain text and isn't re-scanned for more `!` placeholders.

## Frontmatter and `allowed-tools`

`allowed-tools` pre-approves tools for the turn that invokes the command. It accepts a space- or comma-separated string or a YAML list:

```yaml
---
description: Stage and commit the current changes
disable-model-invocation: true
allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *) Bash(git status *)
---
```

- `Bash(git add *)` allows `git add` with any arguments. `Bash(name)` without a `*` matches the exact command.
- Injected commands are checked against your permission rules and don't prompt. A command that isn't allowed, including one a rule would normally ask about, aborts the invocation. Pre-approve it here to avoid that. Deny rules still override `allowed-tools`.
- The grant lasts until your next message.
- Commands in `.claude/commands/` accept the same frontmatter fields except `name` and `paths`.

## Arguments

- `$ARGUMENTS`: the full argument string as typed.
- `$ARGUMENTS[N]` or `$N`: a 0-based positional argument. Quote multi-word values, as in `/my-skill "hello world" second`.
- `$name`: a named argument declared with `arguments: [issue, branch]` in the frontmatter, mapped by position.
- If no placeholder receives the arguments, Claude Code appends `ARGUMENTS: <value>` to the content.
- Escape a literal dollar sign with a backslash, as in `\$1.00`.

---
description: Fix a GitHub issue

Fix GitHub issue $ARGUMENTS. Branch name: $1

A plugin manifest is the `plugin.json` file in a plugin's `.claude-plugin/` directory. It carries the plugin's metadata and the [`userConfig`](#user-configuration) values that Claude Code prompts the user for. It also declares any component that you define inline or keep outside its [default location](#standard-layout).

This reference is for plugin creators, and for marketplace owners who put component fields in a marketplace entry.

`marketplace.json` is the file that defines a plugin marketplace. It contains the marketplace's name, its owner, and one entry per plugin. Each entry's plugin source says where Claude Code fetches that plugin from.

A marketplace source is a separate object that says where Claude Code fetches the marketplace file itself. You write one in settings, or Claude Code builds one when you run `claude plugin marketplace add`.

This reference is for marketplace maintainers who need an exact field name or value, and for administrators who need to know which `source` values are valid in [`extraKnownMarketplaces`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#extraknownmarketplaces), [`strictKnownMarketplaces`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#strictknownmarketplaces), and [`blockedMarketplaces`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/org#restrict-what-users-can-install).

> * **Allowlist and blocklist recipes**: see [Manage plugins for your organization](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/org.md)

* **The marketplace file**: [Top-level fields](#top-level-fields) and [Plugin entries](#plugin-entries)

## Marketplace file

Save the marketplace file at `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` in your marketplace's directory. If you keep the file somewhere else in the repository, users have to declare the marketplace in [`extraKnownMarketplaces`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#extraknownmarketplaces) with `path` set on its source, because `claude plugin marketplace add` has no option for it.

The directory that contains `.claude-plugin/` is called the marketplace root, and every relative plugin source resolves from it, not from `.claude-plugin/`.

Each user registers one marketplace per `name`, so a user can't have two marketplaces with the same name registered at once.

Claude Code ignores an unknown top-level key or plugin-entry key rather than rejecting it, so a typo loads silently. `claude plugin validate` reports each unknown key as a warning.

You can't give your marketplace any of the following names:

* **Official marketplace names**: `claude-code-marketplace`, `claude-code-plugins`, `claude-plugins-official`, `anthropic-marketplace`, `anthropic-plugins`, `agent-skills`, `anthropic-agent-skills`, `life-sciences`, `knowledge-work-plugins`, `claude-for-legal`, `claude-for-financial-services`, `financial-services-plugins`, `first-party-plugins`, and `claude-tag-plugins`. In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), Stop hooks receive `stop_hook_active`, `last_assistant_message`, `background_tasks`, and `session_crons`. The `stop_hook_active` field is `true` when Claude Code is already continuing as a result of a stop hook. Claude Code applies an 8-consecutive-continuation cap: after stop hooks have continued the turn eight times in a row, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn. | Reason | Description |

Field details:

- **`type`** (required): `"http"`.
- **`url`** (required): "URL to send the POST request to."
- **`headers`** (optional): "Additional HTTP headers as key-value pairs. Values support environment variable interpolation using `$VAR_NAME` or `${VAR_NAME}` syntax. Only variables listed in `allowedEnvVars` are resolved."
- **`allowedEnvVars`** (optional): "List of environment variable names that may be interpolated into header values. References to unlisted variables are replaced with empty strings."
- **`timeout`** (common field): Defaults to 600 seconds for HTTP hooks. Claude Code lowers the default to 30 on `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreModelSwitch`, and `PostModelSwitch`, and to 10 on `MessageDisplay`.
- **`statusMessage`** and **`if`** (common fields): A spinner message while the hook runs, and a permission-rule filter for tool events.

Yes, it's the same JSON. The page says: "Claude Code sends the hook's JSON input as the POST request body with `Content-Type: application/json`." The input is the same as what command hooks receive on stdin, including the common fields and the event-specific fields.

The response body uses the same JSON output format as command hooks. Per "HTTP response handling":

- **2xx with an empty body**: "success, equivalent to exit code 0 with no output." So a 200 with no body is a success.
- **2xx with a JSON object body**: "parsed using the same JSON output schema as command hooks. A body that fails schema validation is a non-blocking error."
- **2xx with any other body, such as plain text**: "non-blocking error, handled the same as a non-2xx status. Claude Code doesn't add the text to Claude's context."

To block a tool call or deny a permission, return a 2xx with a JSON body containing the appropriate decision fields.

## Errors and failures

By default, failures are non-blocking:

- **Non-2xx status**: non-blocking error.
- **Connection failure**: non-blocking error.
- **Timeout**: the hook is canceled, and its output is discarded.

After a non-blocking error, the action proceeds. On events such as `PreToolUse`, the page says a non-blocking error shows a `<hook name> hook error` notice in the transcript. It doesn't say exactly how HTTP errors are displayed, so that's likely but not confirmed.

- The connection fails, or the response status isn't 2xx.
- The hook reaches its timeout.
- A 2xx body is neither empty nor a JSON object.

With `"block"`, a failure does what exit code 2 does on that event. The exception is `PermissionRequest`, where it denies the request. The field has no effect on `Stop`, `SubagentStop`, `TaskCompleted`, and `TeammateIdle`.

Two settings apply to HTTP hooks from every source:

- `allowedHttpHookUrls`: when defined at any settings level, an HTTP hook runs only if its URL matches the merged allowlist.
- `httpHookAllowedEnvVars`: when defined, only the listed variables are interpolated into hook headers.
